An association, because dog owners outnumber cat owners
Nothing useful, because a mosaic plot shows counts rather than percents within groups

items.q: In a random sample of 250 adults, 48 of the 120 who exercise weekly said they usually sleep 8 hours, compared with 26 of the 130 who do not exercise weekly. Build a description of the association in context.

claim.label: Association
options: A higher percent of weekly exercisers usually sleep 8 hours than of adults who do not exercise weekly
A lower percent of weekly exercisers usually sleep 8 hours than of adults who do not exercise weekly
Exercising weekly and sleeping 8 hours are not associated

why.1: Compare the percents: 40% is greater than 20%.
why.2: The percents differ (40% and 20%), so there is an association.

evidence.label: Numbers
options: 40% (48 of 120) compared with 20% (26 of 130)
48 people compared with 26 people
74 of the 250 adults sleep 8 hours

why.1: Raw counts mislead when the groups differ in size; give each group's percent.
why.2: That is the overall share; it does not compare the groups.

conclude.model: In this sample, exercising weekly and sleeping 8 hours are associated: 40% of the adults who exercise weekly (48 of 120) usually sleep 8 hours, compared with 20% of the adults who do not (26 of 130).

There is no association, because a survey is unable to measure homework

items.q: A cafe recorded 180 orders. In the morning there were 80 coffee and 25 tea orders; in the afternoon, 30 coffee and 45 tea orders (invented data). Build a statement that compares tea orders in the morning and the afternoon.

claim.label: Comparison
options: A greater share of afternoon orders than morning orders were tea
A greater share of morning orders than afternoon orders were tea
Time of day and type of drink are not associated

why.1: 60% of afternoon orders were tea, compared with about 24% of morning orders.
why.2: The shares differ a lot (60% and 24%), so they are associated.

evidence.label: Numbers
options: 60% (45 of 75) compared with about 24% (25 of 105)
45 tea orders compared with 25 tea orders
About 39% of all 180 orders were tea

why.1: Counts mislead when the groups differ in size; use each group's share.
why.2: That is the marginal share; it does not compare morning with afternoon.

conclude.model: At this cafe, a greater share of afternoon orders were tea: 60% of afternoon orders (45 of 75) compared with about 24% of morning orders (25 of 105), so time of day and drink are associated.

options: Repeating a real experiment on people until the result is clear
Collecting a random sample from a population and computing a statistic
Guessing a likely result from experience before collecting any data

0.09, because estimates from more trials stay closer to the true value
Each is equally trustworthy, since both used the same model

items.q: To study families with 4 children, a student simulates 200 families, using a coin flip for each child (heads for a girl). In 62 of the 200 simulated families, 3 or more of the children were girls. Estimate the chance that a family of 4 children has 3 or more girls.

mistakes.why: That divides by the 800 simulated children. A trial is a family, so divide by the 200 families.
That is 3 girls out of 4 children, the result being counted, not its estimated chance.

items.q: A student council of 8 seniors and 12 juniors says it picked 4 members at random to go to a conference, and all 4 chosen were seniors. In 100 simulated random picks of 4 members, only 2 picked 4 seniors. Build a conclusion about the claim.

evidence.label: Estimate
options: The estimated chance of 4 seniors in a random pick is about 0.02
The estimated chance of 4 seniors in a random pick is about 0.4
The chance of 4 seniors is 4 out of 20, or 0.2

why.1: 0.4 is the share of the council who are seniors (8 of 20), not the chance that all 4 picks are seniors.
why.2: Use the simulation: 2 of 100 trials, about 0.02.

claim.label: Conclusion
options: so a random pick rarely gives 4 seniors, which gives reason to doubt the pick was random
so the pick was certainly not random
so 4 seniors is a typical result of a random pick

why.1: Rare is not impossible: 2 of 100 random picks did give 4 seniors.
why.2: Only 2 of 100 trials gave 4 seniors, which is rare, not typical.

conclude.model: In the simulation only 2 of 100 random picks chose 4 seniors, an estimated chance of about 0.02. Because getting 4 seniors by chance is so unusual, this gives reason to doubt that the council picked the members at random.

items.q: Put the steps of a simulation in order.

It gives success a 6-in-10 chance, not a 1-in-6 chance
It should use 2-digit numbers, because 6 is a 1-digit number
The digit 0 should have been counted as a success, too

items.q: What is the probability that the sum of the two dice is 7?

mistakes.why: That treats the 11 possible sums (2 to 12) as equally likely. They are not: count outcomes in the grid of 36.
That counts (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4) but not their reverses. (6, 1) is a different outcome from (1, 6): the dice are different colors.

items.q: What is the probability that the sum is at least 10?

mistakes.why: That counts only part of the event: a sum of exactly 10 (3 outcomes), or only the sums above 10 (3 outcomes). "At least 10" means 10, 11 or 12, which is 6 outcomes.

<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>36</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{6}{36}</annotation></semantics></math>
<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>5</mn><mn>36</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{5}{36}</annotation></semantics></math>
<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>35</mn><mn>36</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{35}{36}</annotation></semantics></math>

items.q: What is the probability that at least one of the dice shows a 6?

mistakes.why: That counts (6, 6) twice, once for each die. It is one outcome, so there are 11.

items.q: A student says, "There are 11 possible sums, from 2 to 12, so the probability of a sum of 12 is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>11</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{11}</annotation></semantics></math>." What is wrong?

items.q: The coffee shop claims that 30% of its customers use the app. In a random sample of 10 customers, 7 used it. If the claim is true, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.0106</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(A \ge 7) \approx 0.0106</annotation></semantics></math>, with A binomial, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n = 10</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p = 0.3</annotation></semantics></math>. Build a conclusion about the claim.

evidence.label: Probability
options: If 30% of customers use the app, the chance that 7 or more of 10 random customers do is about 0.011
The chance that 30% of customers use the app is about 0.011
The chance that exactly 7 of 10 customers use the app is 0.7

why.1: The 0.011 is computed assuming the claim; it is not the chance that the claim is true.
why.2: 7 of 10 is the sample share, not a probability from the model.

claim.label: Conclusion
options: so this sample gives reason to doubt the claim and suggests more than 30% use the app
so the claim is shown to be false
so the sample is consistent with the claim

why.1: An unusual result casts doubt on a claim; it does not show it false for certain.
why.2: A result this unusual under the claim is not consistent with it.

conclude.model: If 30% of customers use the app, the probability that 7 or more of 10 randomly chosen customers use it is about 0.011. Because that is so unlikely, this sample gives reason to doubt the claim and suggests that more than 30% of customers use the app.

Build a conclusion about the pharmacy's statement.

evidence.label: Probability
options: If the mean wait is 5 minutes, a sample mean of 7.5 or more for 40 customers has probability about 0.0008
The probability that the mean wait is 5 minutes is about 0.0008
About 0.08% of single customers wait 7.5 minutes or more

why.1: The probability assumes the pharmacy's mean; it is not the chance the mean is 5.
why.2: It is about sample means of 40, not single waits.

claim.label: Conclusion
options: so the sample gives strong reason to doubt that the mean wait is 5 minutes
so the mean wait is shown to be exactly 7.5 minutes
so the sample is typical of a mean wait of 5 minutes

why.1: One sample does not pin the mean down exactly.
why.2: A result more than 3 SDs out is not typical.

conclude.model: If the pharmacy's mean wait were 5 minutes, a random sample of 40 customers would have a mean wait of 7.5 minutes or more with probability only about 0.0008. Because that is so unlikely, the sample gives strong reason to doubt that the mean wait is 5 minutes.
